client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Everything just feels kind of gray and hollow — like I go through the motions of my day but nothing actually feels good or meaningful anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I guess I'm here because I didn't know what else to do.
therapist: It takes real courage to show up even when you're not sure it will help, and I want you to know that what you're feeling — that grayness, that hollowness — makes complete sense after losing someone you loved. Grief has a way of muting the world, and it doesn't mean something is permanently broken in you or in your life. I'm really glad you're here, and I'd love to understand more — can you tell me a little about your grandmother and what she meant to you?

client: She was just... the one person who always made me feel like I belonged somewhere, you know? Like no matter what was going on, I could call her and she'd listen without judging me, and somehow everything felt a little more manageable after. Now that she's gone, I keep reaching for my phone to call her and then remembering, and that moment of remembering just hits me all over again every single time.
therapist: That image of reaching for your phone and then remembering — that's one of the most tender and painful parts of grief, and it speaks to how real and alive your connection with her still is inside you. She sounds like she was a truly rare presence, someone who gave you a sense of safety and belonging that's incredibly precious. I'm wondering — when you think about what she gave you in those phone calls, that feeling of being heard and grounded, do you notice any part of you that still carries some of that, even now?

client: I want to say yes, but honestly it just feels like... no, not really. Like whatever that feeling was, it lived in her, and now it's just gone with her. I know that probably sounds like I'm being dramatic, but I genuinely don't know how to access that sense of calm or safety without her being on the other end of that phone.
therapist: That doesn't sound dramatic at all — it sounds like a really honest and painful truth about how much she anchored you, and it makes sense that right now the calm feels like it belonged to her rather than to you. But I want to gently offer a different possibility: that feeling of being heard and safe was real, and *you* were the one experiencing it, which means some part of you knows what it feels like from the inside. I'm curious — when she listened to you without judgment, what do you think she saw in you that made her respond to you the way she did?

client: I guess she saw someone worth listening to, someone she loved... but it's hard to hold onto that right now because I keep thinking about all the times I didn't call when I should have, or cut conversations short because I was busy. Like, what if I wasted so much of the time we had, and now I'm just supposed to carry forward this idea that she believed in me when I'm not sure I deserve that?
therapist: What you just shared is so important, and I want to name what I'm noticing — underneath the grief, there's also a voice telling you that you don't deserve the love she had for you, and that's a really heavy thing to carry alongside the loss itself. It's worth gently asking that voice: do you think your grandmother, who listened without judgment, would look at those missed calls and decide you were unworthy of her belief in you — or is it possible she understood, the way people who truly love us usually do? I wonder, if she were on the other end of that phone right now and you told her exactly what you just told me, what do you imagine she would say to you?

client: She would probably say something like "oh, stop that, I knew you were busy and I never once doubted you loved me." And I can almost hear her voice saying it, which is... actually kind of painful in a different way, because it makes me realize she probably wasn't carrying any of this resentment I've been torturing myself with. But even knowing that, I can't seem to just let the guilt go — like intellectually I can follow the logic, but it doesn't reach whatever part of me is actually hurting.
therapist: You just did something really meaningful — you accessed her voice, her actual perspective, and it told you something true and loving, and that gap between knowing something and *feeling* it is one of the most frustrating parts of grief and guilt, so please be gentle with yourself for being there. That place that's still hurting isn't being irrational; it just needs more than logic to heal — it needs time, and repetition, and maybe some compassion directed inward that feels a lot like what she used to offer you from the outside. I'm wondering — what would it look like to try to speak to yourself, even just in small moments, the way she would have spoken to you?

client: Honestly, my first reaction is that it sounds kind of hollow to try to do that for myself, like I'd just be pretending or putting words in her mouth. She had this warmth that I don't think I can manufacture on my own — it came from her actually knowing me, and me talking to myself in her voice just feels like a pale imitation that might actually make me feel worse. I don't know, maybe I'm being too resistant about it, but I guess I'm scared it would just remind me of what's missing rather than actually helping.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense, and I want to be clear — I'm not asking you to manufacture or perform something that feels false, because you're right that a pale imitation isn't what you need. What strikes me though is that you *just* heard her voice naturally, without forcing it, when you imagined what she'd say to you — and it felt real enough to be painful, which actually means it wasn't hollow at all. I'm curious whether the difference might be less about "talking to yourself in her voice" and more about those moments when she surfaces naturally, like she just did — do you think there might be a way to simply notice and stay with those moments rather than pushing them away?

client: That's actually a fair point, because it did come naturally just now and it didn't feel fake in that moment. I think my instinct is usually to shut those moments down pretty quickly because sitting with them feels like it could just pull me under, like if I let myself really feel her presence I'll just end up more devastated when it fades. I guess I'm not sure I trust myself to stay with it without completely falling apart.
therapist: What you just identified is really profound — you've been protecting yourself from the very thing that might also bring some comfort, because the love and the loss are so deeply intertwined right now. And I want to gently challenge the fear of "falling apart," because in this conversation you've already touched her presence, heard her voice, felt the pain of it — and you're still here, still reflecting, still finding words for it, which suggests you may be more capable of holding this than you're giving yourself credit for. I'm wondering — has there ever been a time in your life when you let yourself feel something really difficult and discovered you could survive it, even if it was hard?

client: Yeah, I think when my parents divorced when I was a teenager, I was convinced I wouldn't be able to handle it, and somehow I did get through it even though it was awful. But I guess the difference I keep coming back to is that I had my grandmother then — she was actually part of how I survived that, so it feels different now that she's the one who's gone and I don't have that same safety net. I'm not sure that past version of me is very useful evidence when the person who helped me through hard things is the exact thing I've lost.
therapist: That's a really honest and sharp observation, and I don't want to dismiss it — you're right that she was part of your strength then, and that matters. But I want to reflect something back to you: she didn't go through that divorce for you, she didn't feel your feelings or make your choices — she witnessed you while *you* found a way through, which means some of that resilience was always yours, even if she helped you see it. I'm wondering — what do you think she would say if you told her you were afraid you couldn't survive this without her?

client: She'd probably say something like "you've always been stronger than you think, I've watched you your whole life and I know what you're made of." And hearing that in my head right now is doing something — I don't know, it's making my chest feel tight in a way that's sad but not entirely bad, like there's something real there. I just worry that I'm going to leave this conversation feeling like I touched something important and then go home and lose it again, like I won't be able to find my way back to this on my own.
therapist: That tightness in your chest — that's not you falling apart, that's you actually letting her in for a moment, and it's real and it matters. What you're afraid of losing is actually a skill you're building right now, not a feeling that exists only in this room — and one small thing that might help is writing down her words, the ones that just came to you, so that when the grayness closes back in you have something concrete to return to. What do you think it would feel like to have those words somewhere you could actually reach for them, the way you used to reach for your phone to call her?

client: That parallel actually hits me in a way I wasn't expecting, the reaching for the phone thing — like maybe instead of reaching for her and finding nothing, I could reach for something she actually left behind in me. But I'm also a little worried that writing it down will make it feel too clinical or like a therapy exercise, and then it loses whatever made it feel real just now. I think I'd want it to feel more like... I don't know, like something private between me and her rather than homework.
therapist: I love that reframe — not a therapy exercise, but something private between you and her, which actually feels much truer to who she was and what you had together. It doesn't have to look like anything prescribed — it could be a single note in your phone, a scrap of paper in your wallet, even just her words in your own handwriting somewhere only you would find it. What feels like the most natural way *you* would want to keep something that belonged to the two of you?
